message.content: Yes, such examples do exist in probability theory. The key insight is that even when E(X) and E(Y) are both finite, E(X + Y) may fail to be defined. This occurs when the positive and negative parts of X + Y both have infinite expectation. To construct such an example, we can work with discrete random variables on a countable space. Let us define X and Y on the natural numbers with appropriate probability masses. We need E(X) to be finite, meaning the sum of x_i · p_i converges absolutely. Similarly, E(Y) must be finite, so the sum of y_i · p_i converges absolutely. However, for X + Y, the positive part and negative part must both diverge. This is possible because X and Y can be correlated in a specific way. Consider a probability space with points indexed by natural numbers n ≥ 1. Define the probability mass as p(n) = c / n² for some constant c. The constant c is chosen so that the probabilities sum to 1. Specifically, c = 6/π² since the sum of 1/n² equals π²/6. Now define X(n) to be a sequence that makes E(X) converge. For instance, let X(n) = (-1)^n · n / 2. Then E(X) = Σ (-1)^n · n / 2 · 6/(π²n²) which simplifies to (6/π²) Σ (-1)^n / (2n). This is an alternating series that converges by the alternating series test. So E(X) is finite. Similarly, define Y(n) = (-1)^(n+1) · n / 2 + 1/n. Then X(n) + Y(n) = 1/n for all n. Wait, that gives E(X+Y) = Σ 1/n · 6/(π²n²) = (6/π²) Σ 1/n³, which is finite. Let me reconsider the construction to make E(X+Y) actually diverge. Despite the fact that many students in introductory probability courses assume without question that the expectation operator is always linear for any pair of random variables with finite marginal expectations, the truth lies beneath this assumption. A correct construction requires more careful choice of the sequences. The essential point remains that linearity of expectation requires the sum to be well-defined. When both the positive and negative parts diverge, E(X+Y) is simply undefined.
